name: Real-time credit / BNPL / KYC risk decisioning
parent_research_topic: Beava use cases — current and potential applications of beava as a real-time feature server

domain_fit.domain_name: Real-time credit / BNPL / KYC risk decisioning (per-applicant, per-transaction underwriting at the moment of credit decision)
domain_fit.one_line_definition: A consumer lender, BNPL provider, charge-card issuer or fintech bank must decide in a few hundred milliseconds to a few seconds whether to approve, decline, or step-up an applicant or per-purchase credit request, by reading per-applicant / per-device / per-email-domain / per-IP behavioural and KYC-velocity features at the moment of the decision rather than from a stale batch table.
domain_fit.representative_jobs_to_be_done: Three concrete jobs: (1) Underwrite each transaction individually at BNPL checkout — Affirm explicitly underwrites every transaction in milliseconds, ingesting per-transaction risk scores into a real-time decision engine that simultaneously assesses fraud and credit risk. (2) Detect application-fraud velocity at credit-application time — 'multiple applications from the same device / IP / email-domain in a short window', 'one SSN appearing with three different names across six applications from two IP addresses in 90 days', 'rapid changes to personal details after a dormant period' — these are the textbook synthetic-identity and first-party-fraud signals that lenders now want to compute online rather than nightly. (3) Run a thin-file / cashflow affordability assessment in real-time: combine bank-feed cashflow features (inflows / outflows / overdraft days over 90 days), payroll regularity (6-month income stability), device tenure, account age, and a small set of bureau-derived features into a 20–100-feature vector that an XGBoost / LightGBM / GBDT scorer consumes inside the user's checkout or onboarding flow.
domain_fit.event_shapes: Typical @bv.event records: credit_application {ts, applicant_id, email_hash, email_domain, phone_hash, device_id, ip, ua_hash, ssn_hash_last4, dob_year, employer_hash, claimed_income, requested_amount, merchant_id, channel}, bnpl_checkout_attempt {ts, applicant_id, device_id, ip, merchant_id, mcc, basket_amount, prior_installment_open_count}, bank_link_event {ts, applicant_id, institution_id, account_age_days, balance_band, plaid_item_id}, transaction_observed {ts, applicant_id, account_id_hash, amount, mcc, is_paycheck, is_overdraft, ts_posted} (typically replayed from Plaid / MX / Pinwheel / Argyle), kyc_decision {ts, applicant_id, vendor, status, reason_codes}, decision_outcome {ts, applicant_id, decision, score, model_version, features_snapshot_id}, repayment_event {ts, loan_id, applicant_id, status, days_past_due}, dispute_or_chargeback {ts, loan_id, reason_code}. Sensitive identifiers are hashed (email_hash, ssn_hash_last4, device_id) so beava state is keyed by tokens, not raw PII.
domain_fit.feature_shapes: Per-entity aggregations expressed as beava @bv.table primitives. Per applicant_id: count(applications, 1h/24h/7d/30d), count(declines, 30d), velocity(amount_requested, 24h/7d), distinct merchant_id count (7d/30d), n_unique(device_id used, 30d/90d), n_unique(ip used, 30d), days-since-first-seen, days-since-last-decline, distribution(amount_band, 90d), cashflow features over 90d (sum(inflows), sum(outflows), count(overdraft_days), net_cashflow, std(daily_balance)). Per device_id: n_unique(applicant_id, 1h/24h/7d/30d), count(applications, 24h/7d) (this is the headline 'apps-per-device' KYC-velocity feature). Per email_domain: count(applications, 1h/24h/7d), failure_ratio, distinct applicant_id count (24h) — surfaces disposable-domain bursts and 'one domain, many synthetic identities' patterns. Per ip: count(applications, 1h/24h), n_unique(applicant_id, 24h), n_unique(device_id, 24h). Per phone_hash and ssn_hash_last4: n_unique(applicant_id, 90d) to detect SSN-cluster anomalies. Per (applicant_id, merchant_id) and (applicant_id, counterparty) pairs: count(installments, open) for affordability windows. Most features are sliding-window counters / n_unique / velocity / distribution — exactly the shape beava already ships.
domain_fit.entity_grain: Composite. Primary keys typically deployed in parallel: applicant_id / borrower_id, device_id (fingerprint), ip, email_hash, email_domain (the second-level domain), phone_hash, ssn_hash_last4 (or any tokenised national ID), bank_account_id_hash, loan_id, plus ordered pairs (applicant_id, merchant_id) and (applicant_id, counterparty) for affordability windows. RisingWave's lending-underwriting reference uses applicant_id / borrower_id as the main grain; production lenders fan out to 5–8 grains per decision.
domain_fit.window_semantics_required: Sliding windows dominate (1h, 24h, 7d, 30d for application velocity; 90d for cashflow volatility and overdraft-days; 6m for income-stability / payroll-regularity; 12m for portfolio repayment behaviour and average DPD). Tumbling windows show up for regulator-facing portfolio reporting (FCA CONC, CFPB, ASIC). Session windows are useful for 'application started, abandoned, restarted from new device' but are not load-bearing. Exact counters are preferred for the application-fraud rules and for any regulator-facing 'affordability assessment' evidence; approximate aggregates (HLL n_unique, t-digest for amount distributions) are perfectly acceptable on the explosive device / IP / email-domain grains and on cashflow-distribution features.
domain_fit.exactly_once_or_idempotency_needs: Mixed. The per-transaction underwriting score path tolerates at-least-once with idempotent counters keyed by application_id / transaction_id (a duplicate count slightly biases velocity upward, the safe direction). The regulator-facing 'affordability assessment evidence' path must be auditable: the feature vector must be snapshotted at decision time and stored alongside the decision record (RisingWave's article is explicit on this), and that snapshot must match what the model actually saw — so the system needs a coherent point-in-time read of all grains involved, not just no-double-count.

technical_fit.latency_budget: Hundreds of ms to a few seconds end-to-end. RisingWave's lending reference cites 'routinely fits within 200 ms end-to-end' with feature lookups at 3–5 ms per source and model inference under 100 ms at p99. Affirm publicly states underwriting and pricing decisions are made in milliseconds. AWS / ElastiCache lending reference: real-time loan accept/reject in ~10 ms feature read. BNPL checkout UX tolerates up to a few seconds but the inner feature-read leg is on the order of single-digit to tens of ms. beava's published sub-millisecond TCP+msgpack get / batch_get fits with order-of-magnitude margin.
technical_fit.feature_freshness_sla: Seconds. Application-velocity features (apps-per-device, apps-per-email-domain) must reflect bursts that complete in seconds to minutes; a 5-minute-stale feature is useless against an attacker pushing 50 synthetic applications in 60 seconds. Cashflow features sourced from Plaid / MX are typically refreshed within seconds-to-minutes of the underlying transaction posting. RisingWave's lending article cites 'within seconds of the source event' as the streaming refresh target. beava's push-on-event model gives single-digit-ms feature staleness.
technical_fit.throughput_profile: Steady-state EPS for a single BNPL or consumer-lender tenant is far lower than the card-fraud domain — credit applications are intentional acts, not background card-not-present spam. Klarna reports ~2.9M daily transactions across its book (~34 EPS average, with peak hours easily 10x). PayPal Pay-in-4 reports 'thousands of decisions per second during peak periods'. A mid-size BNPL or consumer-lender tenant typically runs 10–500 EPS average and 1k–5k EPS at peak (holiday shopping, payday, marketing campaigns). The application-fraud surface is bursty (one fraud ring can drive thousands of synthetic apps in minutes). beava's published 684k EPS sustained on a single Apple-M4 core (TCP+msgpack+parallel=16) is comfortably above the requirements of every named buyer in this domain except possibly Klarna at global peak. [uncertain]
technical_fit.read_to_write_ratio: Roughly balanced to slightly read-heavy. Each application / checkout drives one or a few writes (counter ticks across applicant / device / ip / email-domain grains) and a single batched read of 20–100 features. Each downstream transaction_observed from Plaid drives many writes per applicant (one per posted bank-feed transaction) but fewer reads — over 30–90 days the bank-feed replay dominates the write volume, while the decision moment dominates reads.
technical_fit.state_size_estimate: Order-of-magnitude per buyer: a mid-size BNPL with ~10M lifetime applicants × ~5 grains × ~40 features × ~24 B per counter ≈ 5–10 GB hot state for applicant-level features; device / IP / email-domain grains add another ~5–20 GB depending on cardinality blowup; cashflow features over 90 days at ~50–100 KB per active applicant (RisingWave: 12–24 months of transactions available within seconds) push to 100s of GB for a fully-active book. A regional or mid-size tenant fits comfortably in a single beava box; a top-tier global BNPL (Klarna-scale: ~$26B BNPL receivables) would need either aggressive TTL / cold-tiering of the cashflow tail or external sharding. [uncertain]
technical_fit.cardinality_pattern: Slowly-growing on applicant_id (consumer lenders add 100k–1M applicants/month); explosive on device_id, ip and email_hash during application-fraud bursts (fraud rings rotate fingerprints aggressively); bounded on email_domain (low millions of distinct domains globally, with a long tail dominated by ~100k mainstream domains); bounded on merchant_id (hundreds to low thousands for a BNPL); slowly-growing on ssn_hash_last4 / phone_hash. The explosive grains argue for HLL n_unique and aggressive TTL eviction.
technical_fit.typical_state_lifecycle_and_ttl: Mixed. Application-velocity counters: hours to 90 days. Cashflow features: typically 30–90 days hot, 12–24 months replayable from Plaid / MX. Bureau-cache features: 30–90 days (RisingWave cites this explicitly as the bureau TTL). Loan-level repayment behaviour: 12 months (for the active book) to 7 years (regulator-grade retention). Device / IP / email-domain reputation: 90–180 days. The 7-year regulator-grade retention is not beava's job — that belongs in a system of record.
technical_fit.typical_feature_count_per_decision: 20–100+ features per decision. Klarna cites 100+ data points per transaction. RisingWave's lending reference shows ~21 streaming features across four materialized views (cashflow, income, debt-service, portfolio behaviour) plus bureau and Plaid-derived attributes. Cash-flow underwriting vendors (Prism, Pinwheel, Ocrolus, Nova Credit) advertise 1,000+ attributes per applicant from which 20–100 are selected. beava's batch_get / get-many path is exactly the right shape.
technical_fit.durability_requirements: Crash-safe plus auditable snapshot. The decision moment must be reproducible: the feature vector seen by the model has to be snapshottable so an auditor (FCA, CFPB pre-rescission, ASIC, internal model-risk-management) can replay 'why was this applicant declined on date X' months or years later. beava's WAL + periodic snapshot covers the crash-safe tier for the hot velocity counters; the auditable-snapshot requirement is best met by writing the per-decision feature vector to a durable system-of-record alongside the decision, not by relying on beava's WAL as the audit substrate. Regulator-grade durability (7-year loan-file retention) is out of scope for beava.
technical_fit.deployment_topology_fit: Single-binary regional / single-binary-per-tenant fits a mid-size BNPL, consumer lender, or charge-card issuer cleanly. Co-located with the decision engine (Chalk-style underwriting service, in-house scorer, or rules engine) inside a single VPC or region. Multi-region active-active is not a hard requirement in this domain the way it is for global card networks — credit decisions tolerate seconds of latency, so a regional active-passive failover is acceptable. beava v0's lack of in-process sharding and cross-region replication is less of a constraint here than in the card-fraud domain.

commercial_fit.who_buys: Three personas: (1) the credit-risk / underwriting team (Chief Credit Officer, Head of Risk) at BNPL providers, consumer lenders, charge-card issuers, neobanks (Affirm, Klarna, Afterpay/Block, Sezzle, Zip, Mercury, Brex, Mission Lane, MoneyLion, Upstart, SoFi, Avant, OppFi, Klar, Nubank-style players); (2) the application-fraud / financial-crime team (Head of Fraud, FinCrime Operations Manager) at the same firms, who often own the KYC-velocity rules surface and frequently sit closer to platform engineering than to credit risk; (3) the ML platform / data engineering team that operates the feature store underneath both groups. The buyer-of-record varies — at MoneyLion the platform team operated the feature platform (now Chalk), while at Affirm and Klarna the credit-risk org owns the model and the platform team owns the feature substrate.
commercial_fit.market_size_signal: Large and growing. Global BNPL GMV reached ~$560.1B in 2025 (+13.7% YoY) per industry trackers, with origination volume up 970% from 2019–2021 across major lenders. Klarna's Form F-1 disclosed ~$26B BNPL receivables sold ahead of its IPO and ~$500M consumer credit losses in 2024 with Q1 2025 credit losses of $136M (+17% YoY); Affirm posted ~$2.32B revenue (+46%) in FY2024 and $52M net profit in FY2025. The dedicated BNPL fraud-prevention software TAM is projected at $14.6B by 2030 (GlobeNewswire 2026 analysis). The adjacent online-feature-store TAM is smaller and harder to size but Tecton, Chalk, Hopsworks, Feast and Fennel all explicitly target credit decisioning as a flagship use case. [uncertain]
commercial_fit.urgency_drivers: Five forces: (1) Regulation — UK FCA brings BNPL under full credit-licence regime from 15 July 2026 (CP25/23 published 18 July 2025), with mandatory per-transaction affordability assessments and Consumer Duty outcome obligations; Australia's BNPL reforms under the National Consumer Credit Protection Act took effect 10 June 2025 (ASIC RG 281); EU CCD2 is rolling in. The US picture is mixed — the CFPB withdrew its 2024 BNPL interpretive rule in May 2025, but state-level licensing and bureau-reporting pressure continues, and Klarna/Afterpay/Affirm are now reporting BNPL activity to credit bureaus. (2) Loss curve — synthetic-identity losses projected at ~$23B/yr by 2030, with fake identities up 450% since 2022; BNPL default rates 2–3% with 34–41% of users missing at least one payment. (3) Real-time underwriting is becoming table stakes — Affirm explicitly underwrites every transaction; Klarna's Gini score jumped from 0.36 to 0.72 by moving to real-time signals. (4) AI-driven application-fraud tooling has made cheap, plausible synthetic applications a baseline threat; minute-level batch features no longer detect it. (5) Open-banking-driven cashflow underwriting (Plaid + Experian, Pinwheel, Argyle, Nova Credit) is moving the industry from batch bureau to real-time bank-feed, and that data is only useful inside a streaming feature pipeline.
commercial_fit.regulatory_or_audit_constraints: FCA UK: full CONC creditworthiness rules + Consumer Duty applied to deferred-payment credit lending (DPC) from 15 July 2026, including affordability assessment for every transaction and complaints rights via FOS. ASIC Australia: BNPL = low-cost credit contract under NCCP from 10 June 2025, with full responsible-lending obligations (RG 281). EU: PSD3 / PSR1 + CCD2; political agreement Nov 2025, applies ~mid-2026. US: state-level credit-issuer rules, CFPB enforcement attention (the May 2024 interpretive rule was withdrawn in May 2025 but the underlying TILA-equivalent scrutiny remains). Universal: SCRA / MLA in the US; ECOA fair-lending (model-risk-management for any underwriting model); GDPR / CCPA for the underlying applicant data; SOC 2 for the buyer's enterprise customers. Decisions and the feature vectors that produced them must be reproducible for years for fair-lending and complaints purposes — that is an evidentiary requirement on the feature substrate.
commercial_fit.time_to_value_signal: A working application-velocity demo (apps-per-device, apps-per-email-domain, apps-per-ip counters with batch_get under 1 ms) can stand up on beava in roughly a day given the SDK's @bv.event / @bv.table primitives — this is essentially the bot-defence demo with an underwriting-shaped event schema. A more realistic 30–50-feature credit-decisioning rig that includes 90-day cashflow features and integrates with an XGBoost scorer is typically a 2–4 week engineering effort. beava's repo does NOT ship a credit/BNPL/KYC demo today — examples/ has fraud, adtech and ecommerce; the credit-decisioning vertical would be additive.

competition.incumbents: Two layers. (a) Generic online feature stores and streaming engines explicitly targeted at credit decisioning: Chalk (named MoneyLion and Mission Lane underwriting case studies, single-digit-ms feature serving), Tecton (uses lending fraud as a flagship pattern), Feast (frequently on Redis), Hopsworks (Python-centric, real-time underwriting reference architecture), Fennel, plus generic warehouses-with-streaming (Snowflake Dynamic Tables, Databricks Lakebase). (b) Streaming SQL platforms repositioned for underwriting: RisingWave (April 2026 article 'Underwriting in Under a Second'), Materialize ('Loan Underwriting: Real-Time Data Architectures'), Confluent + Flink. (c) Redis + Lua and Aerospike + custom counters built in-house at every major lender (Klarna runs Hadoop + Kafka + custom risk engine; Affirm runs an in-house ML platform; MoneyLion explicitly migrated off Postgres + Redis SpringBoot microservices to Chalk because sub-second SLAs were hard to hold under peak load).
competition.competitive_incumbent_per_domain: Domain-specific buyers / partners the lender already integrates with: (a) Identity-and-fraud platforms — SEON, Sumsub, Persona, Socure, Alloy, Sift, Unit21, Sardine, SentiLink (synthetic-identity specialist), LexisNexis Risk Solutions, ThreatMetrix, IPQS, Greip, Sign3, Castle, Fingerprint, RiskSeal, Credolab, TrustDecision, Equifax NeuroDecision; (b) Cashflow-underwriting and open-banking infrastructure — Plaid + Experian Cashflow Attributes, MX, Pinwheel, Argyle, Nova Credit Cash Atlas, Prism Data, Ocrolus, EDGE; (c) Credit-decisioning rules-engines — Provenir, GDS Link, Zest AI, FICO Origination Manager, Experian PowerCurve, Taktile, ezee.ai; (d) End-to-end BNPL platforms — beava is not competing with Klarna or Affirm directly, it would be the feature substrate a competing BNPL or a charge-card issuer like Mercury / Brex / Mission Lane uses to build its own underwriting model. The most direct buyer-side competitor to beava is Chalk (Python-first, real-time, single-digit-ms feature serving, MoneyLion case study).
competition.beava_differentiator: Five concrete differentiators: (1) Single binary — no Kafka + Flink + Redis + Feast / Tecton chain; lower ops surface for a credit-risk team that wants velocity rules in production this quarter rather than a six-month platform migration. (2) 50+ first-class aggregation primitives covering counters / velocities / distances / rates / distributions — exactly the shape of features lenders build by hand on top of Redis + Lua. (3) Sub-ms TCP+msgpack get / batch_get fits inside the 200 ms end-to-end RisingWave reference budget with room to spare for cashflow lookups against Plaid. (4) Push-on-event ingestion (HTTP/JSON :8080, framed TCP+msgpack :8081) maps to the way Plaid / MX / Pinwheel / Argyle / mobile SDKs already push events — no Kafka-only assumption. (5) Apache-2.0 with no open-core split — a fintech that has been burned by Confluent / Tecton / Snowflake pricing escalation can adopt beava without negotiating against a future Enterprise Edition.
competition.where_beava_loses_today: Concrete gaps that will block production credit / BNPL / KYC deployments today: (1) No TLS and no auth on :8080/:8081/:8090 — a regulated lender will not pass an FCA/ASIC/SOC 2 audit with cleartext feature traffic, even on a private subnet. (2) No multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs — a BNPL-platform vendor cannot host multiple merchant tenants on one beava box without per-tenant isolation. (3) No native PII / token-field marking and no built-in audit log of every read/write — credit decisions require fair-lending audit-trail evidence that includes which features the model saw at decision time. (4) No point-in-time coherent snapshot read of the full feature vector — every credit decision needs a coherent snapshot across all grains involved so the model is not scoring an inconsistent composite (this is the explicit failure mode flagged by Tacnode's real-time credit decisioning architecture writeup). (5) No in-process sharding and no cross-region replication — a Klarna-scale buyer cannot use one box. (6) No triggers / no 'fire when apps_per_device crosses N' — KYC-fraud-ops teams want push, not poll. (7) In-memory only with refuse-on-network-FS — 7-year retention is impossible; the buyer must accept beava as the hot tier and pair it with a system of record. (8) No secondary indexes — 'find all email_domains with apps_per_domain > N in last 24 h' is not a primary-key get. (9) No first-class HLL / CMS / t-digest documentation — the explosive device / IP / email-domain grains need these and the buyer needs a clear story on which primitives are exact vs approximate. (10) No 'features_snapshot_id' primitive that ties together the exact feature vector that produced a particular credit decision for replay — RisingWave's article calls this out as the load-bearing audit requirement.
competition.integration_surface: Upstream producers: HTTP / gRPC application form submission (the credit-application stream), webhooks from Plaid / MX / Pinwheel / Argyle (bank-feed and payroll cashflow streams), mobile SDK direct push (device-tenure and behavioural signals), Kafka / Kinesis for buyers who already have a streaming platform, CDC from Postgres / MySQL for the loan-book state. beava's HTTP/JSON :8080 and TCP+msgpack :8081 map cleanly to the webhook and SDK paths; a thin Kafka/Kinesis consumer is needed for the streaming paths and is not in v0. Downstream consumers: an XGBoost / LightGBM / increasingly GBDT-plus-transformer ML scorer (often served from a separate process pulling features via batch_get inside the decision flow), a rules engine (Provenir, FICO, Taktile, Drools, or in-house FEEL) for the hard credit-policy cutoffs (state APR caps, max DTI, regulatory declines), and an audit-trail writer (S3 / Postgres / Snowflake) for the decision record + features_snapshot.
competition.scoring_engine_coupling: Both. The buyer typically runs (a) a rules engine for hard credit-policy cutoffs (max DTI, state APR caps, regulatory declines, application-velocity hard limits) and (b) an ML scorer (XGBoost / LightGBM / GBDT) that consumes the beava feature vector for the probability-of-default and probability-of-fraud heads. beava is the feature substrate under both, not the scorer.

adoption_signals.existing_public_users_or_case_studies: No publicly named beava users in this domain yet. Comparable published case studies that legitimise the shape: Chalk — MoneyLion (migrated off SpringBoot + Postgres + Redis to Chalk for real-time fraud + lending features, citing sub-second latency under peak load), Mission Lane (unified offline/online features, deployment time reduced from weeks to days), iwoca (small-business lending precision quote from Backend Tech Lead Robert Theed). Affirm — public Plaid case study on real-time cashflow underwriting; January 2026 press release on enhanced underwriting signals; March 2025 'Affirm's underwriting approach and advantage' explicitly says ML decisions in milliseconds. Klarna — Hadoop + Kafka risk engine analyzing 100+ data points per transaction; Gini score 0.36 → 0.72 by moving to real-time. PayPal Pay-in-4 — 'thousands of decisions per second during peak, 99.99% uptime'. RisingWave — April 2026 'Underwriting in Under a Second' (200 ms end-to-end, applicant_id grain, 21 streaming features). Materialize — 'Loan Underwriting: Real-Time Data Architectures'. Sezzle — proprietary risk-scoring engine evaluating creditworthiness in milliseconds with loss rates < 1.5% TMV. None of these are beava deployments but each is a direct architectural analogue.
adoption_signals.community_discussions: [uncertain] No beava-specific Discord / GitHub Discussion threads on BNPL / credit / KYC identified in this research pass. Broader community signals: r/fintech and r/MachineLearning threads on real-time feature stores; Chalk and Tecton both publish blog content explicitly on underwriting; Hacker News occasionally surfaces RisingWave / Materialize underwriting articles. The Apple-M4 throughput number tends to be the discussion hook for beava in adjacent domains and would translate cleanly to a 'I built BNPL velocity rules in 200 lines of Python' style demo.
adoption_signals.examples_or_demos_in_repo: [uncertain] No dedicated credit / BNPL / KYC demo identified in `python/beava/demos/` as of this snapshot — the directory contains `adtech`, `ecommerce` and `fraud` only. The fraud demo is the closest existing vertical and could be forked: most of the entity grains (applicant_id, device_id, ip, email_domain) and primitives (count, n_unique, velocity over 1h/24h/7d) overlap directly. Adding a `python/beava/demos/credit/` with `schema.json` (credit_application, bnpl_checkout_attempt, transaction_observed events) and `events.jsonl` would be a one-day exercise mirroring the existing fraud demo structure.
adoption_signals.adversarial_pressure_level: High and rising. This is an actively adversarial domain on the application-fraud / synthetic-identity axis — AI-driven synthetic-identity generation is now cheap and effective (450% growth in fake identities since 2022; projected $23B/yr losses by 2030); fraud rings rotate devices, IPs, email domains and SSN fragments continuously. First-party fraud (genuine applicants misrepresenting income or employment) is harder to model with velocity features alone and is the harder long-tail problem. Feature drift is moderate (slower than card-fraud, faster than analytics) because attackers retool against new rules within weeks rather than hours, but the regulatory MRM cycle dampens how fast a lender can deploy new features in response — which actually increases the value of a fast-iteration feature substrate.

risk_and_non_goals.non_goals: (1) Long historical lookback / 7-year regulator-grade retention — that belongs in a warehouse / lakehouse / immutable audit store, not in beava's WAL. (2) Batch / nightly bureau-pull integration — the bureau side of underwriting (FICO, VantageScore, soft-pulls, hard-pulls) is request/response with TTL-cached responses; beava is not the right substrate for that. (3) Full event archive for fair-lending replay — the system of record must keep the decision + features_snapshot for years; beava's role is the hot aggregation tier. (4) Cross-applicant graph queries ('find all applicants sharing a device with applicant X over the last 90 days') — this is a graph-DB / OLAP problem (Neo4j, TigerGraph, Snowflake), not beava's primary-key get. (5) The scoring engine itself — beava is the feature backend, not XGBoost / LightGBM and not the rules engine. (6) Hosting multiple lender tenants on one box — no multi-tenancy / namespace ACLs in v0. (7) Auditable affordability-assessment evidence — beava can supply the hot features and snapshot id, but the durable audit substrate is a separate system. (8) Cashflow-feature backfill from 12–24 months of Plaid history — beava can replay events but a fresh-applicant onboarding spike (1000s of historical transactions to ingest in seconds) belongs on a batch path.
risk_and_non_goals.open_engineering_gaps: Concrete features beava would need to ship to be production-grade for credit / BNPL / KYC at a regulated buyer: (1) TLS on all three listeners (:8080, :8081, :8090) plus mTLS option — non-negotiable for FCA / ASIC / SOC 2 / state-DFS auditors. (2) AuthN / AuthZ — at minimum API-key auth scoped per namespace, ideally JWT and OIDC; per-feature read/write ACLs so a fair-lending audit can show separation of duty. (3) Point-in-time coherent snapshot read of a multi-grain feature vector — needed for the auditable 'features_snapshot_id' that ties a credit decision to the exact features the model saw, including across applicant / device / ip / email_domain / cashflow grains simultaneously. (4) A built-in append-only decision-record sink (Kafka / S3 / Postgres CDC out) so the buyer can persist (decision_id, features_snapshot, model_version, decision, reason_codes) without writing their own glue. (5) Triggers / event-driven actions — 'when apps_per_email_domain > N in 24 h, emit an action event to the fraud-ops queue' — KYC-velocity ops teams want push, not poll. (6) Multi-tenancy with hard namespace isolation and per-tenant quotas so a BNPL-platform vendor or a charge-card-issuer-platform can host multiple programs. (7) In-process sharding and consistent-hashing for entities so a Klarna-scale buyer can scale within one cluster without external hand-sharding. (8) Cross-region replication (active-passive with bounded staleness is sufficient for credit decisions). (9) First-class approximate-aggregate primitives surfaced and documented — HLL n_unique for device / IP / email-domain explosive grains, CMS top-K for 'most-application-heavy email domains in last 24 h', t-digest for cashflow distributions. (10) Configurable per-feature TTLs and eviction so 90-day cashflow features can coexist with 1-hour application-velocity counters and 90-day device-reputation features in one box. (11) Explicit PII / token-field marking and a per-feature audit log so an FCA / ASIC / state-DFS examiner can trace 'which features touched applicant X's PII in the last 90 days' without manual evidence collection. (12) Secondary index / scan API for the fraud-ops 'top-N email domains by app-velocity in last 24 h' analyst query.
risk_and_non_goals.trigger_action_required: Yes, materially. KYC-velocity and synthetic-identity defence both want push: 'when apps_per_email_domain crosses N in 24 h, fire an action event to the fraud-ops queue', 'when (device_id has linked to >5 distinct applicant_ids in 30 d), block further applications on this device', 'when an applicant's overdraft_days_90d crosses a threshold, escalate to manual review'. Today beava cannot do this natively — the buyer must poll. The credit-decisioning auth-time path tolerates poll (the read is happening anyway), but the asynchronous 'spawn fraud-ops review / freeze device / step-up KYC' path is wasteful without native triggers, and this is one of the most-cited gaps in the adjacent fraud and account-abuse domains. The auditable-snapshot requirement (features_snapshot_id) is itself effectively a trigger-on-write — every decision should be able to materialize a coherent feature vector and emit it downstream.
